vision.oneLine: How a bank and an NBFC are audited, from appointment to reports, and the limits that separate one from the other.
vision.why:
Two units, one idea: public money needs a rulebook, and the auditor checks the rulebook was followed. Examiners love this chapter because it is full of thresholds that can be twisted (90 days, 12 or 18 months, 9% or 15%, 2 years, 60 days) and because one line in the study material can be turned into a full case.

It also pays twice: NPA classification, capital ratios and provisioning come back in FR (Ind AS 109 credit losses) and in AFM (credit and risk topics).
vision.marks: about 7 marks an attempt in the 5-year sweep

sixty: A bank takes demand deposits and sits in the payment system. An NBFC lends or invests and cannot take demand deposits.
Banks: appointed with RBI approval; SCAs and SBAs; five stages of audit.
DTL is the base for CRR and SLR: owners' funds and RBI money out; unbooked deposit interest, net credit branch balances and foreign borrowings in.
Drawing power: stock less damaged less creditors, after margin, plus eligible debtors after margin. Stock statement under 3 months old.
NPA means overdue more than 90 days, for banks and NBFCs. Income only on realisation. Classify the borrower, not the facility.
Sale of an NPA: 2 years as NPA, cash, no recourse. Above NBV is not profit.
Capital: bank 9%. NBFC 15% total, Tier I 10%, gold-loan Tier I 12%.
NBFC test: financial assets over 50% and financial income over 50%. CoR plus NOF to start.
Layers: Base (small or special), Middle (deposit-takers and over ₹1,000 crore), Upper (RBI-identified), Top (empty).
Doubtful after 12 months (Middle, Upper) or 18 months (Base). Provision 100% unsecured; 20/30/50% secured; 10% sub-standard.
Reports: banks give LFAR; NBFCs give a Board report and an exception report. CARO 2020 skips banks, covers NBFCs.

askedAs.how: DTL, CRR/SLR, drawing power, CRAR or risk-weighted assets, NBFC provision, 50-50 test, NPA sale loss.
A fact pattern with a stale statement, a guarantee, a consortium or a restructuring. Decide NPA or not, then say why.
Special features, concurrent audit, LFAR, Report to the Board, layers, types of NBFC.
Four-line facts where one threshold decides the answer.
A passing line in the study material (dormant accounts, ROU assets, perpetual debt cap) becomes a full question.

pitfalls: Mixing the bank 9% with the NBFC 15%, or applying the Base Layer 18-month clock to a Middle Layer NBFC.
Treating a Central Government guarantee and a State Government guarantee alike.
Booking the excess over NBV on an NPA sale as profit.
Using 50% as passing in the principal-business test: it must exceed 50%.

levels.title: The big picture: why banks and NBFCs are different
levels.hook: Start here. Every later limit makes sense once you know whose money is at stake.

teach.html: A bank holds other people's money and promises to hand it back on demand. A trader who loses his own money hurts himself. A bank that loses depositors' money hurts thousands of families at once. That is why RBI watches banks so closely, and why the auditor has to check compliance with RBI's rules, not only whether the numbers add up.

teach.h: Six things that make a bank hard to audit
teach.html:
• Cash and negotiable instruments in large volumes.
  • Huge number of transactions, so everything runs on IT.
  • Many branches with decentralised authority.
  • Off-balance-sheet promises (guarantees, LCs) that may involve no accounting entry.
  • A deal started in one place, recorded in a second and managed in a third.
  • Transactions the customer completes alone (ATM, net, mobile).

Bank = takes demand deposits, sits inside the payment system, licensed under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 (RBI Act, 1934 gives RBI power to direct every bank).

NBFC = a company that lends or invests but is not a bank. It lives under Chapter IIIB of the RBI Act, 1934 and needs a Certificate of Registration, not a banking licence.

levels.correlate: Every limit in this chapter comes in a bank version and an NBFC version (CRAR 9% vs 15%, NPA ladder, extra reports). Levels 2 to 10 build the bank side, 11 to 14 the NBFC side, and level 15 puts them side by side.

recall.q: Which Act prescribes the Third Schedule forms (Form A balance sheet, Form B profit and loss) for a banking company?
recall.why: The BR Act, 1949 prescribes Form A and Form B in its Third Schedule and the s.30 audit requirement. The RBI Act gives RBI its power to direct.

recall.q: An NBFC may accept demand deposits from the public.
recall.why: NBFCs cannot accept demand deposits. Some may accept term deposits only (NBFC-D).

recall.q: Which of these is NOT one of the reasons a bank needs special audit attention?
opts: Large volumes of cash and negotiable instruments
Transactions the customer completes alone through ATM or mobile banking
The bank always has a single branch
Off-balance-sheet commitments with no accounting entry
recall.why: Banks have a wide network of dispersed branches with decentralised authority, which is the opposite of a single branch.

recall.q: DICGC deposit insurance is available to depositors of NBFCs.
recall.why: DICGC cover is a bank feature. NBFC depositors have no DICGC insurance.

recall.q: An NBFC is registered under which provision?
recall.why: s.45-IA, RBI Act, 1934: no NBFC can carry on business without a Certificate of Registration and the minimum Net Owned Fund.

twist.q: A company lends to small businesses and also lets customers keep money in on-demand accounts, withdrawable any time. Can it call itself an NBFC?
twist.a: No. Demand deposits are the dividing line. A company that accepts deposits repayable on demand is doing banking business and needs a banking licence. An NBFC can at most take term deposits (NBFC-D), and only if RBI allows it.

levels.title: Who audits a bank, and the five stages
levels.hook: SCA, SBA, indebtedness declaration, internal assignments: classic short-note questions.

teach.html:
Statutory Central Auditor (SCA) audits the bank as a whole at head office level. Most public sector banks appoint four or more firms jointly.

Statutory Branch Auditor (SBA) audits one branch. It is always a single firm. Branch work feeds the central audit.

Section 30(1), BR Act: audit must be by a person qualified to audit companies.

A banking company appoints at the AGM. A nationalised bank appoints through its Board. In both cases RBI approval comes before the appointment.

Before accepting: (1) written declaration of indebtedness: no wilful defaulter status for the firm, partners or family, plus the s.141 Companies Act disqualification declaration; (2) no internal assignments with that bank in the same year; (3) communicate in writing with the previous auditor (Clause (8), Part I, First Schedule, CA Act).

teach.h: The five stages of the audit
teach.html: I Initial considerations, II Understanding, III Risk assessment, IV Execution, V Reporting. Think I-U-R-E-R: "I Understand, Risk it, Execute, Report".

levels.picture:
StageWhat happens
I InitialAcceptance, indebtedness declaration, internal-assignment bar, SA 210 terms, previous auditor
II UnderstandingBank, environment, internal control, accounting and risk-management process
III Risk assessmentSA 315 risks, SA 240 fraud incl. money laundering, IT and outsourcing risk
IV ExecutionSA 330 responses, SA 300 strategy, materiality, going concern
V ReportingAuditor's report and LFAR
levels.correlate: Private banks centralise accounting, so there is no mandatory branch audit for them. NBFCs have no SCA/SBA split at all: one statutory auditor under the Companies Act (Level 14).

recall.q: Put the five stages of a bank audit in order.
recall.why: I-U-R-E-R: Initial, Understanding, Risk assessment, Execution, Reporting.

recall.q: A statutory branch audit can be done by several firms jointly.
recall.why: Joint appointment is for central audit. A branch audit is always by a single firm.

recall.q: A firm that did internal assignments for a bank in the year wants the statutory audit of the same bank. Result?
opts: Allowed if fees are below a limit
recall.why: RBI bars a firm associated with internal assignments in that bank during the same year from the statutory audit.

recall.q: The "declaration of indebtedness" confirms that…
opts: the bank owes nothing to the auditor
the auditor, firm, partners and family are not declared wilful defaulters by any bank or FI
the auditor has no loan above ₹1 crore
recall.why: It is a wilful-defaulter confirmation, in addition to the s.141 Companies Act declaration.

recall.q: RBI approval is needed before a bank appoints its statutory auditors.
recall.why: Whether appointed at the AGM or by the Board, RBI approval comes first.

twist.q: The question says: "Stage III assesses fraud risk incl. money laundering." A student writes SA 330 as the standard. Right or wrong?
twist.a: Wrong. Fraud risk is SA 240 (plus RBI KYC/AML norms). SA 330 is the Stage IV response to assessed risks. When a question names an activity, first place it in a stage (III vs IV), then name the SA.

levels.title: Controls at the counter: cash, clearing, advances, IT
levels.hook: Internal-control questions list 3 to 5 lapses. Learn the safe version of each.

teach.html: Cash sits in the joint custody of two responsible officers. It is test-checked daily, counted in full now and then by an officer other than the handler, and agreed to the day book every day. The cashier must have no access to the customer ledger or day book: someone who can both take cash and change the ledger can hide a theft.
CTS clearing, bills for collection and bills purchased each need independent reconciliation. For inward clearing items of ₹5 lakh and above, the bank contacts the customer before honouring.

Appraise creditworthiness, sanction within authority, execute documents before disbursal, keep a margin, hold security in joint custody of two officers, register charges, keep the account within drawing power and limit. An additional temporary limit is at most 20% of the existing limit for at most 90 days. Every account is reviewed at least once a year.
Because almost everything runs on systems, check access control, change management, backup, interface controls between applications and outsourced services.

levels.correlate: These controls decide how much substantive testing you do on advances in Level 5, and whether a stale stock statement turns an account into an NPA in Level 6.

recall.q: Maximum additional temporary limit on an advance account?
recall.why: 20% of the existing limit and 90 days of tenure.

recall.q: The cashier may also keep the customer ledger to save staff.
recall.why: The cashier must have no access to the customer ledger or the day book.

recall.q: Documents (agreement, DPN, hypothecation letter) should be executed…
recall.why: Documents are executed before the money leaves the bank.

recall.q: Inward clearing cheques at or above how many ₹ lakh trigger customer contact?
recall.why: The SM threshold is ₹5 lakh and above.

recall.q: Securities held against advances should be in the custody of one senior officer for accountability.
recall.why: Joint custody of two officers, not one.

twist.q: A branch gives a customer an ad hoc limit of 30% of his sanctioned limit for four months, and the account is not reviewed for 14 months. List the lapses.
twist.a: (1) Temporary limit above 20%. (2) Tenure above 90 days. (3) No annual review. Each lapse is a separate mark. Also note that repeated ad hoc limits can be used to dodge the 180-day review rule that makes an account an NPA (Level 6).

levels.title: Liquidity plumbing: DTL, CRR and SLR
levels.hook: DTL is the base. Get the exclusions and inclusions right and the numericals are easy.

teach.h: Picture a bank as a shop with a cash box
teach.html: DTL (Demand and Time Liabilities) is what the bank owes to the public, now or later. CRR is a share of DTL kept as cash with RBI. SLR is a share of DTL kept in liquid assets (cash, gold, approved government securities) in the bank's own hands. CRR protects RBI's control of money; SLR protects the depositor if there is a run.

teach.h: Take OUT: money that is not owed to the public
teach.html:
• Paid-up capital, reserves, credit balance in P&L
  • Loans from RBI; refinance from EXIM, NHB, NABARD, SIDBI
  • Net income-tax provision
  • Bills discounted with RBI-approved FIs; amounts from DICGC/ECGC pending claims; court receivers
  • Part recoveries on bad debts; margins in sundry deposits (as in PYQ Nov 2024)

Memory: owners' money and the central bank's money are out.

teach.h: Put IN even if not yet booked
teach.html:
• Net credit balance in branch adjustment accounts (a debit balance adds nothing)
  • Interest accrued on deposits, calculated each reporting fortnight
  • Borrowings from abroad, at gross
  • Cash collateral under collateralised derivatives

Branches send Friday trial balances; head office consolidates. SLR is verified on 12 odd dates in different months, none a Friday. CRR return is Form A, SLR return Form VIII. Reporting runs through the Automated Data Flow (ADF).

levels.picture:
OUT of DTLIN to DTL
Capital, reserves, P&L creditNet credit in branch adjustment
RBI loan, EXIM/NHB/NABARD/SIDBI refinanceInterest accrued on deposits (booked or not)
Net income-tax provisionBorrowings from abroad (gross)
DICGC/ECGC, court receiversCash collateral on derivatives
levels.correlate: NBFCs have no CRR/SLR. Their safety net is the capital ratio (Level 13). A bank's safety net has two layers: liquidity (CRR/SLR, this level) and capital (CRAR, Level 8).

recall.q: Paid-up capital and reserves are part of DTL.
recall.why: Owners' funds are excluded from DTL.

recall.q: Interest accrued on deposits but not yet booked still counts in DTL.
recall.why: It is included whether or not it has been accounted for, so the true liability is reflected.

recall.q: SLR compliance is verified on…
opts: 12 odd dates in different months, none a Friday
the last day of each quarter only
recall.why: RBI requires 12 odd dates in different months, none a Friday.

recall.q: DTL = reported ₹1,000 crore less ₹400 crore excluded items plus ₹20 crore unbooked deposit interest. What is DTL in ₹ crore?
Which return reports CRR?
recall.why: Form A is CRR; Form VIII is SLR. NBS-7 is the NBFC capital return.

twist.q: The branch adjustment account shows a net debit balance of ₹40 crore instead of a credit. Does DTL fall by ₹40 crore?
twist.a: No. Only a net credit balance is included. A net debit simply adds nothing; it is not deducted. So DTL is lower than in the credit case by the credit that is no longer added, not by an extra deduction. Always read the direction of the balance.

levels.title: Advances and drawing power
levels.hook: The biggest asset line in a bank, and the most tested numerical: drawing power.

teach.h: What you are really checking on advances
teach.html: Five assertions: the amount is outstanding at year end, it is due to the bank and backed by loan documents, nothing is unrecorded, the value reflects recoverability, and provisions follow RBI norms.

teach.h: Drawing power: how much the bank will lend against today
teach.html:
DP is worked out from the security: stock paid for, plus eligible debtors, less the margin. Rules that win marks:

  • Remove damaged or obsolete stock.
  • Remove sundry creditors for goods (stock not yet paid for is not the borrower's).
  • Debtors: remove those older than the stipulated period (for example over 90 days).
  • Apply the margin to what is left.
  • Stock statement must be no older than 3 months.
  • In a consortium the lead bank's DP calculation binds members.

Examine all large advances, sample the rest. Look at SMA-1 and SMA-2 accounts that are not yet NPAs, accounts flagged by concurrent audit or RBI inspection, and restructured accounts. Stock audit (including book debts) is mandatory above a stipulated funded-exposure limit.

levels.picture: DP = (Stock − damaged − creditors) × (1 − stock margin) + (Debtors − old debtors) × (1 − debtor margin). Usable = lower of DP and sanctioned limit.
levels.correlate: If outstanding is above DP the account is irregular. If it stays out of order for more than 90 days, it becomes an NPA (Level 6). The same stock statement that sets DP also decides whether a "temporary deficiency" excuse works.

recall.q: Which item is deducted from stock when computing drawing power?
recall.why: Stock bought on credit is not yet the borrower's money; creditors for goods are deducted along with damaged stock.

recall.q: Net eligible stock ₹400 lakh, margin 25%. Stock DP in ₹ lakh?
A stock statement 5 months old can support DP.
recall.why: The statement must be no older than 3 months.

recall.q: In a consortium, each member bank must accept the lead bank's DP calculation.
recall.why: The lead bank's calculation and allocation bind the members (but classification as NPA is each bank's own call).

recall.q: DP works out to ₹504 lakh and the sanctioned limit is ₹450 lakh. The bank can allow…
recall.why: The lower of DP and limit.

twist.q: Stock ₹500 lakh (₹40 lakh damaged), debtors ₹400 lakh (₹60 lakh over 90 days), creditors for stock ₹60 lakh, margins 25% on stock and 40% on debtors. Limit ₹600 lakh. The borrower asks for ₹540 lakh. Can the bank give it?
twist.a: Stock: 500 − 40 − 60 = 400 × 75% = 300. Debtors: 400 − 60 = 340 × 60% = 204. DP = 504. Limit 600 does not bind. Allowed = 504, so ₹540 lakh is ₹36 lakh above DP: irregular, to be reported. Try the Step Solver version to practise this.

levels.title: The NPA ladder in banks
levels.hook: The highest-scoring topic of the chapter (5-year sweep). Know the traps.

teach.html: Standard (performing), Sub-standard, Doubtful, Loss. An account becomes an NPA when it is overdue for more than 90 days (or the other facility-specific triggers). Move down a box as the account stays bad: a bank keeps an NPA in sub-standard for 12 months and then calls it doubtful (RBI IRAC norms; the SM does not print this number, check it).

If one facility of a borrower goes bad, all that borrower's facilities are classified as NPA. Bank classifies on its own experience in a consortium: a lead bank's "performing" certificate does not bind you (SM TYK 5).

• Temporary deficiency (stale stock statement, balance a little over limit, delayed renewal) is not NPA by itself, if the statement is under 3 months old and the account has not been out of order for over 90 days.
  • Limit not reviewed within 180 days of the due date or ad hoc sanction: NPA.
  • Central Government guarantee: NPA only after the guarantee is invoked and repudiated. State Government guarantee follows the normal 90-day rule.
  • Restructured standard account is downgraded to sub-standard; a restructured NPA keeps its category.
  • Upgrade: check every NPA to standard upgrade; look for partial recoveries dressed up as regularisation.
Once an account is NPA, interest is booked only when realised. Interest already credited but unrealised is reversed. Dividends: accrue only once declared at the AGM.

levels.picture:

1 to 30SMA-0 (early warning, still standard)

More than 90NPA (sub-standard first)

SMA bands are RBI's early-warning framework (Beyond the SM; the SM only says SMA-1 and SMA-2 accounts must be examined).
levels.correlate: NBFCs use the same 90-day trigger and the same four boxes, but the sub-standard to doubtful clock is 12 months (Middle/Upper layer) or 18 months (Base layer). Banks: 12 months. See Level 13.

recall.q: An account is an NPA once overdue for more than how many days?
recall.why: 90 days, for banks and for NBFCs.

recall.q: A Central Government guaranteed advance becomes NPA the day it is 91 days overdue.
recall.why: Only once the guarantee is invoked and repudiated. State Government guarantees follow the normal rule.

recall.q: A limit has not been reviewed for 200 days after its due date. Status?
recall.why: Not reviewed within 180 days of the due date or ad hoc sanction means NPA.

recall.q: Interest on an NPA is taken to income on accrual because it is legally due.
recall.why: Only on realisation. Previously credited unrealised interest is reversed.

recall.q: In a consortium, the lead bank certifies X Ltd as performing, but your bank's own experience is poor. You…
opts: classify on your own experience of recovery
classify only your share after a year
recall.why: Each member bank classifies the advance it has given on its own experience.

twist.q: X Ltd owes the bank two facilities. Facility A (term loan) is 100 days overdue; facility B (cash credit) is regular. How is B classified?
twist.a: Borrower-wise classification: since A is NPA, B is also NPA, even though it is regular. Classify the borrower, not the facility. (The auditor then checks that income on B is also treated on the NPA basis.)

levels.title: Selling NPAs and the provisioning idea
levels.hook: RTP May 2025 and SM TYK repeat the same trap: what to do with the excess over book value.

teach.h: Five conditions to sell an NPA
teach.html: (a) Held as NPA for at least 2 years; (b) sold without recourse; (c) the bank keeps no residual risk; (d) cash basis, whole price upfront; (e) the bank has not bought back an NPA it earlier sold.

NBV = outstanding − provision held. If the sale price is below NBV, the shortfall is debited to that year's P&L. If it is above NBV, the excess is not profit and the excess provision is not reversed: it is kept to absorb losses on sale of other NPAs.
The buying bank classifies and provides on its own. Recoveries first go to acquisition cost; only the excess is profit. Risk weight for capital adequacy: 100%.

Provision is the bank's admission that part of a loan will not come back. The worse and less secured the loan, the higher the percentage. Standard assets also carry a small prudential provision at sector-wise rates. Bank percentages are not in the SM; the NBFC percentages are (Level 13).

levels.correlate: The sale price test links to Level 6 (how long it has been NPA) and Level 8 (a purchased NPA has a 100% risk weight in the buyer's CRAR).

recall.q: Minimum years an account must have been NPA before it can be sold?
recall.why: Two years in the selling bank's books.

recall.q: Outstanding ₹10 crore, provision held ₹6 crore, sale price ₹3 crore. Loss to be debited to P&L (₹ crore)?
recall.why: NBV = 10 − 6 = 4. Shortfall = 4 − 3 = 1.

recall.q: If an NPA is sold above NBV, the excess is shown as profit and excess provision is written back.
recall.why: Excess is not recognised as profit and excess provision is not reversed; it covers shortfalls on other NPA sales.

recall.q: A bank may sell an NPA for part cash now and the rest depending on future recovery.
recall.why: Cash basis only, entire consideration upfront, no contingent price.

recall.q: Risk weight on an NPA purchased from another bank?
recall.why: 100% for capital adequacy.

twist.q: A bank sells an NPA that has been in its books as NPA for 18 months, at a price above NBV. A colleague argues the excess is fine to book as profit "since it is above book". Rebut in two lines.
twist.a: First, the sale itself is not allowed: 18 months is below the 2-year minimum. Second, even a valid sale above NBV gives no profit and no write-back of excess provision. Check eligibility before arithmetic.

levels.title: Capital adequacy: CRAR and risk weights (banks)
levels.hook: Capital is the cushion that absorbs losses. Learn Tier I vs Tier II and how risk weights shrink assets.

teach.html: CRAR = (Tier I + Tier II capital) ÷ (risk-weighted assets + risk-adjusted off-balance-sheet items) × 100. RBI minimum for banks: 9% on an ongoing basis (built on Basel III).

A ₹100 government security is almost safe; a ₹100 unsecured loan is not. Weights turn each rupee of asset into "risky rupees". Example in the SM: secured housing loan up to ₹75 lakh = 50%; above ₹75 lakh = 75%; commercial real estate = 100%. A ₹60 lakh housing loan adds only ₹30 lakh to the denominator.

Tier I: share capital and disclosed reserves: best quality, absorbs loss while the bank is still running. Tier II: some reserves and subordinated debt: weaker. Basel III aims: stronger shock absorption, better risk governance, more transparency.

levels.correlate: Same formula in NBFCs, but the bar is higher: 15% total and 10% Tier I (12% for gold-loan NBFCs). Bank 9, NBFC 15. This single contrast is the most common mix-up.

recall.q: Minimum CRAR for banks (%)?
recall.why: 9% per the SM. NBFCs need 15%.

recall.q: Housing loans of ₹200 crore (each up to ₹75 lakh) at 50% risk weight contribute how much to RWA (₹ crore)?
Tier I ₹30 crore, Tier II ₹6 crore, RWA ₹400 crore. CRAR (%)?
Tier II capital absorbs losses better than Tier I.
recall.why: Tier I is the highest quality and fully loss-absorbing.

recall.q: The risk weight on a commercial real estate exposure in the SM example is…

twist.q: Same bank, but the housing loans are all above ₹75 lakh each. What happens to CRAR?
twist.a: Risk weight rises from 50% to 75%, so RWA rises and CRAR falls with unchanged capital. In the Step Solver example CRAR drops from 9% to about 7.6%, below the minimum. Always read the size of each loan.

levels.title: Liabilities, deposits and the off-balance-sheet traps
levels.hook: Short facts that become full questions: NRI accounts, dormant accounts, window dressing, contingent liabilities.

teach.html:
CASA = current and savings (repayable on demand); term deposits are for a fixed period. FCNR: NRIs, fixed deposits only, foreign currency, interest on a 360-day year. NRE: rupee, repatriable. NRO: any non-resident, not repatriable except current income. Savings accounts are never for business or professional concerns.

Inoperative: no transactions for over 2 years. Bulk deposits: ₹2 crore and above (scheduled commercial banks): check the correct rate and the foreclosure penalty.
Near year end a bank may inflate deposits with overdrafts that are reversed after the year. If you suspect it, qualify the report.

Reserves and surplus heads: statutory reserves, capital reserves, share premium, revenue and other reserves (incl. Investment Fluctuation Reserve), P&L balance. Borrowings: from RBI, other banks, other institutions, outside India; inter-office items are not borrowings; refinance is a borrowing, rediscount is not. Interest accrued but not due goes in other liabilities, not with deposits.

Claims not acknowledged as debts, partly paid investments, forward exchange and derivative contracts, guarantees, acceptances and endorsements, bills for collection. A loss that has already crystallised needs a provision, not a disclosure. Check the forex net position is squared.

levels.correlate: Deposits are also the numerator of DTL (Level 4), and inflated year-end deposits would distort CRR/SLR as well.

recall.q: FCNR deposits can be opened by NRIs as…
recall.why: FCNR is a foreign-currency fixed deposit.

recall.q: An account with no transactions for more than how many years is inoperative?
recall.why: More than 2 years.

recall.q: A proprietary business may open a savings account if turnover is small.
recall.why: Savings accounts are for individuals, HUFs and approved institutions only.

recall.q: Which is shown under borrowings?
recall.why: Refinance is a borrowing; rediscount does not figure here; inter-office items are not borrowings.

recall.q: A claim against the bank that has already crystallised is disclosed as a contingent liability.
recall.why: It needs a provision.

twist.q: Deposits jump 8% in the last week of March and fall back in April. The bank says it is "seasonal". What do you do?
twist.a: Suspect window dressing: test for near-date overdrafts parked as deposits and reversed after year end. If confirmed, qualify the audit report.

levels.title: Reports: statutory report, LFAR, concurrent audit
levels.hook: Who reports what, to whom and by when. Students mix these up under pressure.

teach.html: For a nationalised bank the auditor reports to the Central Government on: explanations given, transactions within the bank's powers, adequacy of branch returns, true profit or loss, a true and fair balance sheet, and anything else. Plus SA 700, 705, 706, 710, 720, and Rule 11 matters (pending litigation, foreseeable losses, IEPF delay, and so on). CARO 2020 does not apply to a banking company.

Both SBAs and SCAs give a Long Form Audit Report: cash, bank balances, investments, advances, deposits and more. Branch LFARs feed the central LFAR. It goes to the Audit Committee of the Board (ACB), and a copy with the Board's views reaches RBI within 60 days.

teach.h: Concurrent audit: audit as it happens
teach.html: Checks transactions as they take place (not a pre-audit), like an internal audit. Scope is set by the Central Inspection and Audit Department with the ACB, high-value and high-risk first. Area: cash, deposits, advances, investments, forex, housekeeping. Tenure of an external concurrent auditor: max 5 years bank-wide, max 3 years at one branch. The ACB fixes remuneration.

Fraud: report under s.143(12) to the Central Government as prescribed; a fraud noticed in the ordinary course is also reported to RBI and the CMD/CEO. SCA certificates include ICFR, SLR compliance, treasury operations, IRAC compliance and CRAR authentication.

levels.title: NBFC: is it one, and how does it enter?
levels.hook: The 50-50 test and the registration numbers decide the first mark of every NBFC question.

teach.html: s.45-I(f), RBI Act: an NBFC is a financial institution that is a company, or a non-banking company whose principal business is receiving deposits or lending, or any other class RBI notifies.

Per the last audited balance sheet: financial assets > 50% of total assets (net of intangibles) and income from financial assets > 50% of gross income. Both must pass. Exactly 50% fails because the rule says "exceeds".

s.45-IA: no NBFC may start without a Certificate of Registration (CoR) and the minimum Net Owned Fund. General minimum NOF is moving to ₹10 crore by 31 March 2027; ₹2 crore for NBFC-P2P, NBFC-AA and NBFCs with no public funds or customer interface; ₹300 crore for NBFC-IFC and IDF-NBFC.

Housing finance institutions (NHB), merchant banking, stock exchanges, stock-broking, VCFs and AIFs (SEBI), Nidhi companies (MCA), insurance companies (IRDA), chit companies, specified micro finance companies, securitisation companies, mutual benefit companies, and certain CICs.
ICC, IFC, CIC, IDF-NBFC, NBFC-MFI, NBFC-Factors, NOFHC. And by deposits: NBFC-D or NBFC-ND.

levels.correlate: Unregistered NBFC business is reported by the auditor under CARO 2020 clause 3(xvi)(a)/(b) (Level 14). The NOF figure decides capital compliance in Level 13.

recall.q: A company with 70% financial assets but only 40% financial income qualifies as an NBFC.
recall.why: Both limbs must exceed 50%.

recall.q: NOF required for NBFC-IFC and IDF-NBFC (₹ crore)?
recall.why: ₹300 crore.

recall.q: General minimum NOF by 31 March 2027?
recall.why: Phased: ₹2 crore → ₹5 crore (by 31.3.2025) → ₹10 crore (by 31.3.2027).

recall.q: Which entity does NOT need NBFC registration?
recall.why: Nidhi companies are regulated by MCA.

recall.q: Total assets ₹600, intangibles ₹80, financial assets ₹260. Financial assets as % of total assets net of intangibles?
recall.why: 260 ÷ 520 = 50%, which does not exceed 50%, so the asset limb fails.

twist.q: ABC Ltd passes the asset test at 76% but its financial income is exactly 50% of gross income. Can it apply for registration?
twist.a: No. The income test needs more than 50%. Exactly 50% fails, so ABC is not an NBFC on the principal-business criteria (and must not carry on NBFC business without registration).

levels.title: NBFC layers: who sits where
levels.hook: The categorisation puzzle. Learn the rule of three: size, activity, RBI identification.

teach.h: The four layers (Scale Based Regulation, from 1 October 2022)
teach.html: The bigger and riskier the NBFC, the heavier the rulebook. Base (smallest or special-purpose), Middle, Upper and Top (ideally empty).
Non-deposit-taking NBFCs below ₹1,000 crore, plus NBFC-P2P, NBFC-AA, NOFHC and NBFCs with no public funds and no customer interface. P2P, AA, NOFHC and no-public-funds NBFCs always stay in Base.
All deposit-taking NBFCs (any size), non-deposit NBFCs of ₹1,000 crore or more, and Standalone Primary Dealers, IDF-NBFCs, CICs, HFCs and NBFC-IFCs. SPD and IDF-NBFC always stay in Middle.
Upper = the NBFCs RBI identifies by a scoring methodology; the top 10 by asset size are always Upper. Top is populated only if RBI sees a big rise in systemic risk from an Upper NBFC.

• Deposit-taking NBFC, CIC, IFC, HFC: Middle or Upper, never Base.
  • Government-owned NBFCs: Base or Middle only (never Upper) for now.
  • ICC, MFI, Factors, MGC: can land in any layer by score.

levels.title: NBFC prudential norms: capital, classification, provisioning
levels.hook: Three tables to know by heart, and the twists that depend on the layer.

teach.html: Minimum capital ratio (Tier I + Tier II) 15% of risk-weighted assets, with Tier I at least 10% at all times. Gold-loan NBFCs (at least 50% of financial assets in gold loans): Tier I at least 12%. Tier II can never exceed Tier I. NBFC-BL cannot count perpetual debt instruments in Tier I or II. Risk weights to remember: cash, bank balances, approved securities, loans to staff, claims on Central Govt: 0%; PSU bank bonds 20%; State-guaranteed claims not in default (or default up to 90 days) 20%; most other loans, investments, fixed assets 100%; retail consumer credit and credit cards 125%.

NPA = overdue more than 90 days (the glide path from 150 and 120 days is over). Sub-standard until the asset has been NPA for 18 months (Base) or 12 months (Middle and Upper); then Doubtful. Loss when the NBFC, its auditor or RBI identifies it as lost.

CategoryProvision
Loss100% (or write off)
Doubtful, unsecured part100%
Doubtful, secured part20% up to 1 year as doubtful, 30% for 1 to 3 years, 50% beyond 3 years

Same as banks: on an NPA, income only on realisation; unrealised income booked earlier is reversed.

levels.correlate: Bank vs NBFC: CRAR 9% vs 15%. Both use the 90-day trigger and the four boxes. The NBFC doubtful clock depends on the layer; the bank clock does not.

recall.q: Minimum Tier I for an NBFC (general), as % of RWA?
recall.why: 10%. Gold-loan NBFCs 12%.

recall.q: An NBFC-BL has a loan NPA for 15 months. Category?
recall.why: Base Layer allows 18 months as sub-standard, so 15 months is still sub-standard.

recall.q: The same loan in a Middle Layer NBFC (15 months NPA) is…
recall.why: Middle and Upper: 12 months, so doubtful.

recall.q: Sub-standard loan ₹5 crore. Provision (₹ crore)?
recall.why: 10% flat on the total outstanding.

recall.q: Standard-asset provision is deducted from gross advances to show net advances.
recall.why: It is shown separately as contingent provision against standard assets, never netted.

twist.q: An NBFC-ML loan of ₹5 crore, realisable security ₹3 crore, has been NPA for 14 months. Provision? Now redo for an NBFC-BL.
twist.a: ML: 14 months > 12, doubtful for 2 months (<1 year). Unsecured 2 × 100% = 2.0; secured 3 × 20% = 0.6; total ₹2.6 crore. BL: 14 < 18, still sub-standard: 10% × 5 = ₹0.5 crore. Same loan, five times the provision; only the layer changed.

levels.title: The NBFC auditor: procedures, reports, CARO, Ind AS format
levels.hook: The reports an NBFC auditor must file and the thresholds for fraud.

teach.html: (1) Scan MOA/AOA and Board minutes to pin down the principal business; (2) evaluate internal control, especially periodic review of advances; (3) verify registration and NOF; (4) verify Public Deposit Directions; (5) verify prudential norms.

A separate report in addition to the s.143 report. All NBFCs: CoR obtained and still justified by the principal-business criteria at year end; NOF met. Deposit-accepting NBFCs: deposit limits, rating, CRAR, no default to depositors, returns on time. Non-deposit NBFCs: Board resolution of non-acceptance, no deposits accepted, CRAR (Form NBS-7). A Statutory Auditor's Certificate on CoR eligibility reaches the RBI DNBS regional office within 5 working days of signing the audit report, and not later than 31 December.

If any matter is unfavourable or the NBFC has not complied with Chapter IIIB, the Public Deposit Directions or the Scale Based Regulation Directions, 2023, send an exception report to the DNBS Regional Office. It reports contraventions only; never a certificate of compliance.

CARO 2020 applies to NBFCs: clause 3(iii) loans, clause 3(xvi) registration (a) required and obtained? (b) business without CoR? (c) CIC criteria? (d) number of CICs in the group. Under Ind AS the NBFC uses Division III: financial and non-financial assets, balance sheet in order of liquidity allowed, separate disclosure of items above 1% of total income.
Cash shortage is fraud if over ₹10,000, or over ₹5,000 when detected by management, the auditor or an inspecting officer and not reported by the cash handler on occurrence.

levels.correlate: Mirror image of Level 10: LFAR (bank) ↔ Report to Board and exception report (NBFC). CARO excluded for banks, applied to NBFCs.

recall.q: Working days within which the Statutory Auditor's Certificate reaches RBI after signing the audit report?
recall.why: 5 working days, and not later than 31 December of the same year.

recall.q: The exception report may state that the NBFC has complied with the Directions.
recall.why: Contraventions only; no statement certifying compliance.

recall.q: Order the five NBFC audit steps.
items: Pin down principal business from MOA, AOA and minutes
recall.why: Business first, then controls, then registration/NOF, deposits, prudential norms.

recall.q: A cash shortage of ₹7,000 is detected by the auditor and was not reported by the cashier on occurrence. Fraud?
opts: Yes, above ₹5,000 and detected by the auditor
recall.why: Above ₹5,000 when detected by management/auditor/inspector and not self-reported.

recall.q: Separate disclosure threshold for other income or expenditure under Division III, as % of total income?
recall.why: 1% of total income. Division II uses 1% of revenue or ₹10 lakh, whichever is higher.

twist.q: Total income ₹10,000 crore; outsourcing cost inside "other expenditure" is ₹99.50 crore. Separate note needed?
twist.a: No. 1% of ₹10,000 crore = ₹100 crore. ₹99.50 crore is 0.995%, which does not exceed 1%, so no separate disclosure is required.

levels.hook: The exam-day consolidation. Use the Compare tab and play the sorter until it is automatic.

teach.h: Seven contrasts to say in your sleep
teach.html:
• CRAR: bank 9%, NBFC 15% (Tier I 10%, gold 12%).
  • Entry: banking licence vs CoR + NOF.
  • Liquidity: CRR/SLR on DTL (bank) vs none (NBFC).
  • Deposits: demand + DICGC (bank) vs term only, no DICGC (NBFC-D).
  • Extra reports: LFAR (bank) vs Board report + exception report (NBFC).
  • CARO 2020: excluded (bank) vs applies (NBFC).
  • Layers: none (bank) vs four (NBFC).
NPA trigger of more than 90 days; Standard/Sub-standard/Doubtful/Loss; income on NPAs only on realisation; standard assets still carry a provision.

teach.h: Updates the printed SM does not show (RTP May 2026)
teach.html: (1) NBFC-MFI must keep at least 60% of total assets (net of intangibles) in microfinance loans, on an ongoing basis; 4 consecutive quarters of shortfall means a remediation plan to RBI. (2) Gold-loan NBFC Tier I follows the RBI (Lending Against Gold and Silver Collateral) Directions, 2025; the 1 April 2026 date has passed. (3) ROU assets now sit in the "Others" line of the NBFC RWA table at 100%.

teach.h: Beyond the SM: concepts a clever examiner can build a question on
teach.html:
These follow from the chapter's ideas; check the latest RBI text before quoting figures.

  • Ind AS 109 and NBFCs: Ind AS NBFCs provide on expected credit loss (ECL). RBI compares ECL with the prudential (IRAC) provision; if ECL is lower, the shortfall goes to an Impairment Reserve out of profit.
  • RBIA: risk-based internal audit looks at risk, not only transactions.
  • SARFAESI: recovery from secured assets without first going to court.
  • Priority sector: banks have lending targets; NBFCs do not.
  • Co-operative banks: also answer to co-operative societies law.

recall.why: They are in the "Others (to be specified)" line at 100%.

solves.title: DTL, then CRR and SLR
solves.tip: Split the list into two piles first: "owners and central bank" (out) and "public and unbooked" (in). Then move the decimal: 4% of 1,550 is 1,550 ÷ 100 × 4.

variants.label: Base case
variants.q: A bank's liabilities (₹ crore): deposits 1,400; other liabilities 100; loans from RBI 100; paid-up capital 60; reserves 240; credit balance in P&L 20; net income-tax provision 30. Total reported: 1,950. Not yet booked: interest accrued on deposits 10. Net credit balance in branch adjustment accounts 40 (not in the 1,950). Assume CRR 4% and SLR 18% for this question.

steps.ask: Which items come OUT? Add RBI loan, capital, reserves, P&L credit and tax provision (₹ crore).
steps.say: 100 + 60 + 240 + 20 + 30 = 450. Owners' funds and central-bank money are excluded.

steps.ask: Reported 1,950 less the excluded items (₹ crore).
Add unbooked deposit interest and net credit in branch adjustment accounts. DTL (₹ crore)?
steps.say: 1,500 + 10 + 40 = 1,550. Both are included even if not booked.

variants.label: Twist 1: net debit
variants.q: Same bank, but the branch adjustment accounts show a net debit balance of 40 instead of a credit. Everything else is the same (CRR 4%, SLR 18%).

steps.ask: How does the net debit balance affect DTL?
opts: Add nothing: only a net credit is included
steps.say: Only a net credit balance is included. A net debit adds nothing.

variants.label: Twist 2: foreign borrowing
variants.q: Back to the base case (net credit 40), but the bank also has borrowings from an overseas bank of 100, not in the 1,950. CRR 4%, SLR 18%.

steps.ask: Are borrowings from abroad included in DTL?
steps.say: Borrowings from abroad are included at gross.

solves.title: Drawing power
solves.tip: Do it as "keep" percentages: margin 25% means keep 75% (three quarters). Margin 40% means keep 60% (three fifths). Clean the base first, then multiply once.

steps.say: 300 + 204 = 504. Limit 600 is higher, so DP governs.

variants.q: Same facts, but the sanctioned limit is only ₹450 lakh and the outstanding is ₹460 lakh.

steps.ask: Maximum the account may draw: lower of DP and limit (₹ lakh).
Outstanding 460: excess over the permitted amount (₹ lakh).

variants.q: Same base facts (limit ₹600 lakh) but the bank raises the stock margin to 30%. Debtor margin stays 40%.

steps.ask: Total DP with debtors DP 204 (₹ lakh).

opts: Yes, the figures are the same

steps.say: A temporary deficiency excuse needs both a fresh statement and not more than 90 days out of order. Over 90 days means NPA.

solves.title: Is it an NPA on 31 March?
solves.tip: Count days by month ends: days left in the start month + full months. From 15 December: 16 + 31 + 28 + 31 = 106. Anything above 90 is an NPA; 61 to 90 is SMA-2 (early warning, still standard).

variants.q: Same loan, but the instalment fell due on 15 January 2026.

steps.say: 75 days is not more than 90: still standard, but in the SMA-2 early-warning band, so the auditor examines it.

variants.label: Twist 2: other facility
variants.q: The borrower has a term loan (instalment due 15 December 2025, unpaid) and a cash credit account which is fully regular.

steps.ask: Classification of the regular cash credit account?
steps.say: Classification is borrower-wise, so all facilities become NPA.

solves.title: NBFC provision: the layer twist
solves.tip: Ask three questions in order: which layer (12 or 18 months)? How long as NPA? Then split the loan into secured and unsecured. Unsecured is always 100%. Compute in crore with round numbers.

variants.label: Base case
variants.q: An NBFC in the Middle Layer has a loan of ₹5 crore that has been NPA for 14 months. Realisable value of security: ₹3 crore.

steps.say: Middle Layer: 12 months as NPA then doubtful. 14 months means doubtful.

steps.ask: For how many months has it been doubtful?
steps.say: 14 − 12 = 2 months, which is under 1 year, so the 20% band applies to the secured part.

steps.ask: Provision on the unsecured portion (₹ crore).
Provision on the secured portion at 20% (₹ crore).

variants.label: Twist 1: Base Layer
variants.q: Same loan, but the NBFC is in the Base Layer.

steps.say: Base Layer: 18 months as sub-standard. 14 months is still sub-standard.

variants.label: Twist 2: old doubtful
variants.q: Middle Layer NBFC, same ₹5 crore loan and ₹3 crore security, but the loan has been NPA for 5 years (60 months).

steps.ask: Years as doubtful (60 months less the first 12).
steps.say: 60 − 12 = 48 months = 4 years, which is over 3 years.

steps.ask: Provision on the secured portion at 50% (₹ crore).
Total provision with the unsecured 2.0 (₹ crore).

solves.title: NBFC capital ratios
solves.tip: Make RWA 1,000 in your head and read every percentage as "tenths of a hundred": Tier I of 100 is 10%, total of 155 is 15.5%. The comparison is then instant.

variants.label: Base case
variants.q: A general NBFC (not gold-loan) has Tier I capital ₹100 crore, Tier II ₹55 crore, risk-weighted assets ₹1,000 crore.

steps.say: 10% ≥ 10% and 15.5% ≥ 15%. Also Tier II (55) does not exceed Tier I (100). Compliant.

variants.label: Twist 1: Tier II falls
variants.q: Same, but Tier II is only ₹45 crore.

steps.say: Total 14.5% is below the 15% minimum: non-compliant, even though Tier I passes.

variants.label: Twist 2: gold-loan NBFC
variants.q: Same base numbers (Tier I 100, Tier II 55, RWA 1,000) but the NBFC lends mainly against gold (more than 50% of financial assets).

steps.say: The gold-loan floor is on Tier I: 100 < 120. Non-compliant.

variants.label: Twist 3: perpetual debt
variants.q: Gold-loan NBFC-BL, RWA ₹1,000 crore, reported Tier I ₹130 crore, which includes ₹25 crore of perpetual debt instruments.

steps.ask: Can an NBFC-BL count perpetual debt in Tier I?
steps.say: NBFC-BL cannot include perpetual debt instruments in Tier I (or Tier II).

steps.ask: Shortfall against the 12% floor of 120 (₹ crore).

solves.title: Bank CRAR with risk weights
solves.tip: Weights first, then add. 0% items vanish; halve the 50% items; keep the 100% items. Bank minimum is 9%, so for RWA 400 you need capital of 36.

variants.label: Base case
variants.q: A bank (₹ crore): cash 100 (0%); government securities 400 (0%); secured housing loans, each up to ₹75 lakh, 300 (50%); corporate loans 200 (100%); off-balance-sheet items, credit equivalent 50 (100%). Capital: Tier I 30, Tier II 6.

steps.ask: Risk-weighted value of the housing loans (₹ crore).
Total RWA including corporate loans 200 and off-balance-sheet 50 (₹ crore).

steps.say: 9% meets the 9% minimum, with no cushion.

variants.label: Twist: larger housing loans
variants.q: Same bank, but all the housing loans are above ₹75 lakh each (weight 75%).

steps.ask: Extra capital needed to reach 9% (₹ crore).

solves.title: Is it an NBFC? The 50-50 test
solves.tip: Net the intangibles from total assets first. Then ask: is the fraction above one half? Compare by doubling the numerator: if 2 × financial assets is more than the denominator, the test is passed.

variants.label: Base case
variants.q: Total assets ₹600 crore, intangible assets ₹100 crore, financial assets ₹300 crore. Gross income ₹100 crore, of which income from financial assets ₹54 crore.

steps.ask: Total assets net of intangibles (₹ crore).
Financial assets as % of net total assets.
Financial income as % of gross income.

steps.say: Both limbs exceed 50%: it qualifies as an NBFC and can apply under s.45-IA.

variants.label: Twist 1: income falls
variants.q: Same company, but income from financial assets is only ₹45 crore of ₹100 crore gross income.

steps.ask: Financial income as % of gross income.

steps.say: Both limbs must pass. Not an NBFC on these figures.

variants.label: Twist 2: exactly 50%
variants.q: Total assets ₹600 crore, intangibles ₹80 crore, financial assets ₹260 crore. Financial income is 60% of gross income.

steps.ask: Financial assets as % of net total assets.

opts: No: the rule needs more than 50%

solves.title: Selling an NPA
solves.tip: Eligibility first (2 years?), arithmetic second. NBV = outstanding minus provision. Compare price with NBV only, never with the outstanding.

variants.label: Base case
variants.q: An account has been NPA for 3 years. Outstanding ₹10 crore; provision held ₹6 crore. Proposed sale for cash, without recourse, at ₹3 crore.

opts: Yes: 3 years ≥ 2 years, cash, no recourse
steps.say: Meets the 2-year, cash and without-recourse conditions.

variants.label: Twist 1: above NBV
variants.q: Same account, but the buyer pays ₹7 crore in cash.

steps.ask: Excess of price over NBV (₹ crore).

opts: Not profit; excess provision retained for losses on other NPA sales
steps.say: The excess is not recognised as profit and the excess provision is not reversed.

variants.label: Twist 2: too young
variants.q: Same numbers, but the account has been NPA for 18 months.

steps.say: Eligibility fails at 18 months. No sale, so no arithmetic needed.

solves.title: Cash shortage: is it a fraud report?
solves.tip: Two doors: over ₹10,000 always reportable. Over ₹5,000 reportable only when someone other than the cash handler found it and the handler did not report it at the time.

variants.label: Base case
variants.q: An NBFC branch has a cash shortage of ₹12,000, reported by the cashier on the same day.

steps.say: Over ₹10,000 is reported as fraud regardless of proven intent.

variants.label: Twist 1
variants.q: Shortage ₹7,000, detected by the auditor; the cashier had not reported it.

opts: Yes: over ₹5,000 and detected by the auditor
steps.say: Over ₹5,000, detected by management/auditor/inspector and not reported by the cash handler on occurrence: fraud report.

variants.label: Twist 2
variants.q: Shortage ₹7,000, reported by the cashier himself on the same day. No sign of intent.

opts: No, unless intent to cheat is suspected or proved
steps.say: Below ₹10,000 and self-reported, so it is reported as fraud only if there is intent.

variants.label: Twist 3
variants.q: Shortage ₹4,000, detected by the auditor, not reported by the cashier.

steps.say: Both thresholds are crossed only above ₹5,000. Below that, intent decides.

solves.title: Division III: the 1% test
solves.tip: 1% means move the decimal two places left. Compare the item with that number. The base is total income, not revenue.

variants.label: Base case
variants.q: Ind AS NBFC, total income ₹10,000 crore, revenue from operations ₹9,900 crore. Manpower outsourcing cost inside other expenditure: ₹99.5 crore.

steps.say: The item must exceed 1% of total income. 99.5 is below 100.

variants.label: Twist: higher cost
variants.q: Same company, but the outsourcing cost is ₹101 crore.

variants.label: Twist: Division II
variants.q: A non-NBFC Ind AS company: revenue from operations ₹10,000 crore. Same ₹101 crore item. Division II threshold is 1% of revenue or ₹10 lakh, whichever is higher.

steps.ask: Threshold in ₹ crore (1% of revenue vs ₹10 lakh = ₹0.1 crore; take the higher).
steps.say: 1% of 10,000 = 100, much higher than 0.1, so the threshold is 100.
Yes, but notice the base changed (revenue, with a ₹10 lakh floor). Division III uses total income.

15% total, 10% Tier I, 12% Tier I for gold-loan NBFCs

mnemonics.story: Baby, Mid, Upper, Top: heavier rules as you grow.

Over ₹10,000 always. Over ₹5,000 if someone other than the cash handler found it.

Financial assets over 50% and financial income over 50%. Exactly 50% fails.

hooks.h: DTL: the bank's IOUs to the public
hooks.story: Imagine the bank as a shopkeeper with a wall of IOUs. Every IOU the public could ask him to honour now or later is DTL. The shopkeeper's own capital and his loan from the central bank are not IOUs to the public, so they are out. Interest he owes but has not written down is still an IOU, so it is in.

hooks.h: The NPA ladder: milk going off
hooks.story: Standard is fresh milk. Over 90 days overdue it is sub-standard: turning. After 12 months (18 in a Base Layer NBFC) it is doubtful: sour, some part may still be saved from the security. Loss is poured away. The unsecured part of a doubtful loan is already poured away (100%).
Base is primary school: light rules. Middle is secondary: deposit-takers and anyone over ₹1,000 crore. Upper is the board exam class: RBI picks by score. Top is the rank list that is normally empty.

Tier I is the car's main shock absorber: it works while the car is moving. Tier II is the spare: it helps, but later. The ratio asks how many shock absorbers per kilometre of risky road (risk-weighted assets). A bank has two other safety nets (CRR and SLR); an NBFC does not, so it needs more shock absorbers (15%).

links.how: Same formula, different bar. The NBFC bar is higher, and it also has a Tier I floor of 10% (12% for gold loans).
The trigger is common. The NBFC glide path (150, 120, then 90 days) is complete.
Realisation basis in both; unrealised income already booked is reversed.
Each world has its extra report beyond the normal audit report. LFAR goes via the ACB to RBI; the Board report goes to the Board, with an exception report to RBI if anything is unfavourable.
Clause 3(xvi) on registration under s.45-IA is an NBFC clause.
Banks have a liquidity net (CRR/SLR) and a capital net. NBFCs have no CRR/SLR, so the capital bar carries more weight.
A statement over 3 months old makes drawing power unreliable; out of order for over 90 days means NPA.
Repeated ad hoc renewals can be used to dodge this rule; the auditor tests review dates.
Interest credited but not realised is reversed; the margin falls.
Same loan, same months: sub-standard in Base, doubtful in Middle or Upper. The provision can be five times higher.
Pass both limbs and you are an NBFC that needs a CoR and NOF; carrying on without them is reported under CARO 3(xvi).
An unfavourable or qualified matter in the Board report triggers the exception report to the DNBS regional office.
Concurrent audit findings go to the ACB quarterly; the ACB reviews LFAR and oversees the whole audit function.
The excess covers shortfalls on other NPA sales.
A purchased NPA enters the buyer's RWA at 100%.

links.a: Perpetual debt above the Tier I cap
links.how: Cap is 15% of prior-year Tier I (non-BL); Tier II can never exceed Tier I; NBFC-BL cannot count it at all.
Only the Central guarantee delays NPA status until it is invoked and repudiated.
Balance sheet in order of liquidity and 1% of total income test apply to Division III.
Ind AS NBFCs provide on ECL; RBI compares it with the prudential provision and any shortfall goes to an Impairment Reserve (Beyond the SM; check current RBI wording).

links.how: Weighting assets by risk is the same idea as sizing credit loss by exposure and probability of default.
